rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should look ahead: lowering the head compromises upright posture, while keeping it erect and looking down is severe hardship, which religion removes.
rows.anchor: إن حنى رأسه ذهب ببعض القيام المعترض عليه في الرأس، وهو أشرف الأعضاء، وإن أقام رأسه وتكلف النظر ببصره إلى الأرض فتلك مشقة عظيمة وحرج،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wherever you are covers every place a person may inhabit.
rows.anchor: وحيث ما كنتم: هذا عموم في الأماكن التي يحلها الإنسان، أي في أي موضع كنتم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, ḥaythu is initially a place adverb with a genitive complement; adding mā removes annexation, gives it conditional force, and lets it govern the verbs.
rows.anchor: فإذا وصلت بما زال منها معنى الإضافة، وضمنت معنى الشرط، وجوزي بها، وصارت إذ ذاك من عوامل الأفعال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to face the Sacred Mosque applies equally to Muhammad and his community, avoiding any impression that the ruling was exclusive to him.
rows.anchor: أراد أن يبين أن حكمه وحكم أمته في ذلك واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is general across the earth, so the qibla is not restricted to Medina.
rows.anchor: فبين أنهم في أيما حصلوا من بقاع الأرض، وجب أن يستقبلوا شطر المسجد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is addressed first because he longed for the change; the community follows him, and this order prevents assuming the command was his alone.
rows.anchor: بدأ بأمره أولا ثم أتبع أمر أمته ثانيا لأنهم تبع له في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh says ‘toward it’ instead of ‘toward its direction.’
rows.anchor: وفي حرف عبد الله: فولوا وجوهكم قبله.

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads ‘in its direction’; these variants show that shatr means toward or in the direction of something.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة: فولوا وجوهكم تلقاءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended sense of shatr is direction or towardness.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله يدل على أن المراد بالشطر: النحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those described as recipients of scripture are the leading Jews and Christians and their learned authorities.
rows.anchor: أي رؤساء اليهود والنصارى وأحبارهم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies the recipients of scripture here as the Jews.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: هم اليهود.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What they know to be true is facing the Sacred Mosque, the direction God prescribed for Abraham and his descendants.
rows.anchor: أي التوجه إلى المسجد الحرام، الحق: الذي فرضه الله على إبراهيم وذريته.

rows.speaker: قتادة والضحاك
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the qibla meant is the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والضحاك: إن القبلة هي الكعبة.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī takes the pronoun to refer to shatr, meaning the direction, close to the preceding explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: الضمير يعود على الشطر، وهو قريب من القول الثاني

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Another view, also given by Qatāda and Mujāhid, takes the pronoun as Muhammad: they know his truthfulness and prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعود على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، أي يعرفون صدقه ونبوته، قاله قتادة أيضا ومجاهد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger pronoun refers to his own address; under this analysis the passage contains two shifts in address.
rows.anchor: ومفسر ضمير الرسول ضمير خطابه صلى الله عليه وسلم. فعلى هذا الوجه يكون التفاتان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān notes that this analysis of the pronouns yields two shifts in address.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا الوجه يكون التفاتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ‘know’ may take two objects or one, since its complement is an أن-clause.
rows.anchor: والعلم هنا يحتمل أن يكون مما يتعدى إلى اثنين

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says they knew from their scripture that the direction was toward the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: إما لأن في كتابهم التوجه إلى الكعبة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that their scripture identifies Muhammad as a true prophet who commands only what is right.
rows.anchor: وإما لأن في كتابهم أن محمدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further basis for their knowledge is that abrogation is permissible.
rows.anchor: وإما لجواز النسخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may also know because prophetic glad tidings said the Messenger would pray facing both qiblas.
rows.anchor: وإما لأن في بشارة الأنبياء أن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘From their Lord’ is a circumstantial phrase meaning that the truth is established by their Lord; the change was commanded by God, not reached through ijtihād.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك دليل على أن التحول من بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God ‘their Lord’ signals that one must follow truth established by the one who cares for one's reform, as ‘the truth is from your Lord’ says.
rows.anchor: كما قال تعالى: الحق من ربك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read the closing verb with second-person tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي بالتاء على الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the second-person reading, the addressees may be believers, following the preceding command to face the mosque.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن يراد به المؤمنون لقوله: فولوا وجوهكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the second-person reading addresses the People of the Book, shifting from third-person reference to direct speech.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يراد به أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct address urges the People of the Book to act on the truth they know; confrontation intensifies blame and underscores the matter's gravity.
rows.anchor: تحريكا لهم بأن يعملوا بما علموا من الحق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers using third-person yāʾ most naturally refer to the People of the Book, continuing the surrounding third-person discourse.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالياء، فالظاهر أنه عائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either reading warns that God does not overlook people's deeds.
rows.anchor: وعلى كلتا القراءتين، فهو إعلام بأن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the People of the Book will not follow the Prophet's qibla consoles him: they know it is true yet conceal it and refuse its consequence.
rows.anchor: ما تبعوا قبلتك هذه تسلية للرسول عن متابعة أهل الكتاب له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their opposition is deliberate stubbornness, so even every miracle would not make them follow him; one miracle would be still less likely to do so.
rows.anchor: لو جئتهم فيها بجميع المعجزات التي كل معجزة منها تقتضي قبول الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Every sign’ means all evidence showing that turning toward the Kaaba is true.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: بكل آية يدل على أن توجهك إلى الكعبة هو الحق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in la-in signals a preceding unexpressed oath; the oath's answer is mā tabiʿū, so it needs no conditional fa, while the conditional answer is omitted.
rows.anchor: واللام في: ولئن، هي التي تؤذن بقسم محذوف متقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although tabiʿū is past in form, it has future sense because the condition is future; the conditional result is suppressed and supplied by the oath answer.
rows.anchor: لأن الشرط قيد في الجملة، والشرط مستقبل، فوجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogous construction in 30:51 likewise uses a past-form verb for a future result, with the conditional answer omitted beneath the oath answer.
rows.anchor: ونظير هذا التركيب في المثبت قوله تعالى: ولئن أرسلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ instead treats in here as law, making mā tabiʿū the conditional answer, just as law can be answered by mā.
rows.anchor: وذهب الفراء إلى أن إن هنا بمعنى لو، ولذلك كانت ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Farrāʾ's analysis, in without the meaning of law normally requires fa in its answer, as in ‘if you visit me, then I will not visit you.’
rows.anchor: وإن كان إن إذا لم يكن بمعنى لو، لم يكن جوابها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows an oath preceding a condition to have its answer supplied by the condition's clause; Abū Ḥayyān says this is not the Basran position.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا مذهب البصريين، بل الجواب يكون للقسم بشرطه المذكور في النحو.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because using in to mean law is rare, Abū Ḥayyān keeps in in its ordinary sense where that reading works.
rows.anchor: واستعمال إن بمعنى لو قليل، فلا ينبغي أن يحمل على ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the oath answer resembles a law answer because the two particles can substitute for one another, though his explanation is unclear.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وجاء جواب لئن كجواب لو، وهي ضدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān finds Ibn ʿAṭiyya inconsistent: his opening makes the answer belong to in, but his later statement says it belongs to the oath.
rows.anchor: لأن أوله يقتضي أن الجواب لإن، وقوله بعد: فالجواب إنما هو للقسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says Ibn ʿAṭiyya's substitution argument explains an in-answer, not an oath-answer, and Sibawayh does not say the two particles substitute.
rows.anchor: والتعليل بعد بقوله، لأن أحد الحرفين يقع موقع الآخر، لا يصلح

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says mā tabiʿū answers the oath, with a past-form verb carrying future meaning.
rows.anchor: إلا أن ما تبعوا جواب القسم، ووضع فيه الماضي موضع المستقبل.

rows.speaker: الأخفش والفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Zajjāj say in and law can each stand in for the other and take the other's answer pattern.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الناس: كل واحدة من: لئن ولو، تقوم مقام الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān summarizes two analyses: Sibawayh makes mā tabiʿū the omitted oath's answer; al-Akhfash, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Zajjāj make it in's answer by treating in like law.
rows.anchor: وتلخص من هذا كله أن في قوله: ما تبعوا قولين: أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surface wording ‘those given scripture’ is general, and some interpreters take it that way here.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: أوتوا الكتاب: العموم، وقد قال به هنا قوم.

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm restricts the People of the Book to the learned group identified earlier and later; the intervening wording also depicts entrenched denial, although many scripturalists believed and followed the qibla.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصم: المراد علماؤهم المخبر عنهم في الآية المتقدمة

rows.speaker: الحسن والجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Jubbāʾī understand ‘they will not follow your qibla’ collectively: the group will never unite in following it, though individuals may.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن والجبائي: أراد جميعهم، كأنه قال: لا يجتمعون

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm instead means that not one individual from the specifically hardened group will believe or follow the qibla.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصم: بل المراد أن أحدا منهم لا يؤمن.

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim argues that God's knowledge of people's acts does not excuse them; they can do commanded good and leave what is forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقد احتج أبو مسلم بهذه الآية، على أن علم الله في عباده

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author's associates use the prediction to support the possibility of imposing an unperformable duty: if they followed, God's truthful report would become false, which is impossible.
rows.anchor: واحتج أصحابنا به على القول بتكليف ما لا يطاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qibla is attributed to God because He prescribed it and is the one followed in facing it.
rows.anchor: وأضاف تعالى القبلة إليه، لأنه المتعبد بها والمقتدى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God disabuses the Prophet of hope in their conversion: they reject from stubbornness, without proof or even doubt, so argument will not dislodge them.
rows.anchor: لأنهم لم يتركوا اتباعه عن دليل لهم وضح، ولا عن شبهة عرضت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some construe ‘you are not one to follow their qibla’ as a prohibition: continue as commanded, though the Prophet is already protected from doing so.
rows.anchor: قيل: ومعناها النهي، أي لا تتبع قبلتهم، ومعناها: الدوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view keeps the sentence declarative: it rules out future abrogation of the new qibla.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي باقية على معنى الخبر، وهو أنه بين بهذا الإخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further declarative reading cuts off the People of the Book's deceptive hope that the Prophet would return to their qibla if they promised belief.
rows.anchor: فجاءت هذه الجملة رفعا لتجويز النسخ، أو قطع بذلك رجاء أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed purposes are to establish the Prophet's immunity, to express the impossibility created by their differing qiblas, or to contrast their attachment to falsehood with his adherence to truth.
rows.anchor: أو بين بذلك حصول عصمته، أو أخبر بذلك على سبيل التعذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular ‘their qibla’ covers the distinct Jewish and Christian qiblas because they share the quality of being false, and the singular also suits the preceding contrast.
rows.anchor: لأنهما اشتركتا في كونهما باطلتين، فصار الاثنان واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This nominal sentence strengthens the denial by repeating the noun and marking the predicate with an emphatic bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة أبلغ في النفي من حيث كانت اسمية تكرر فيها الاسم مرتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence is a new clause linked to the preceding discourse, not merely to the conditional answer, since their condition cannot qualify the Prophet's non-following.
rows.anchor: وهي مستأنفة معطوفة على الكلام قبلها، لا على الجواب وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers attach the active participle to the following noun in an iḍāfa; both this and its operative construction are eloquent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض القراء: بتابع قبلتهم على الإضافة، وكلاهما فصيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘some of them follows another's qibla,’ the pronoun ‘them’ refers to the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: الضمير في بعضهم عائد على أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews do not adopt the Christian qibla, nor Christians the Jewish one; their intense mutual hostility underlies this division, while the author says he saw conversions to Islam but not between them.
rows.anchor: أن اليهود لا يتبعون قبلة النصارى، ولا النصارى تتبع قبلة اليهود

rows.speaker: السدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd say the two groups are the People of the Book who remain in their own religions; the author calls this the apparent reading.
rows.anchor: هذا قول السدي وابن زيد، وهو الظاهر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes one group converts and the other those still in their former faiths, since each disparages and rejects the other's way; Ibn Salām was praised before his conversion was known and slandered afterward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أحد البعضين من آمن من أهل الكتاب، والبعض الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the People of the Book jointly oppose the Prophet, their qiblas differ: Jews face Jerusalem and Christians face sunrise.
rows.anchor: وإن اتفقوا على خلافك، فهم مختلفون في القبلة، وقبلة اليهود بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats following their desires as a hypothetical: after proof was clear, such a choice would be grave injustice; the warning deters listeners from abandoning evidence and urges steadfastness.
rows.anchor: كلام وارد على سبيل الفرض، والتقدير بمعنى: ولئن اتبعتهم مثلا بعد وضوح البرهان

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One reported view takes the warning's addressee to be the Messenger alone.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم: هو للرسول، وقال بعضهم: هو للرسول وغيره.

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reported view addresses both the Messenger and others.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هو للرسول وغيره. وقال بعضهم: هو لغير الرسول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A third view says it addresses someone other than the Messenger, since God knew the Messenger would not do this and would not single him out with the warning.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هو لغير الرسول، لأنه علم تعالى أن الرسول لا يفعل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawā is pluralized as ahwāʾ, not ahwiya; it usually means a harmful desire, though it can mean good, and derives from inclination and love.
rows.anchor: أهواءهم: تقدم أنه جمع هوى، ولا يجمع على أهوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source noun is plural because people's aims and objects of desire differ.
rows.anchor: وجمع، وإن كان أصله المصدر، لاختلاف أغراضهم ومتعلقاتها وتباينها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Knowledge’ means the proofs and signs that produce knowledge; the cause is named by its effect, honoring knowledge and emphasizing its rank.
rows.anchor: أي من الدلائل والآيات التي تفيد لك العلم وتحصله، فأطلق اسم الأثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that a warning directed at learned people is more severe than one directed at others.
rows.anchor: ودلت الآية على أن توجه الوعيد على العلماء أشد من توجهه على غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes ‘knowledge’ here as the truth, namely that the qibla change is right.
rows.anchor: وقد فسر العلم هنا بالحق، يعني أن ما جاءه من تحويل القبلة هو الحق.

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says that ‘knowledge’ here means clarification or exposition.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: العلم هنا: البيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān varies between alladhī, mā, and min after baʿd; Abū Ḥayyān treats the choice as fluent variation, with min marking the beginning of the post-arrival period.
rows.anchor: لأن ما والذي موصولان، فأيا منهما ذكرت، كان فصيحا حسنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says alladhī is more specific and denotes knowledge of Islam's truth, while mā is vaguer and denotes knowledge of a single pillar such as the qibla or scripture.
rows.anchor: لأن الذي أخص، وما أشد إبهاما، فحيث خص بالذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous explanation says min marks the first time the Prophet had to oppose the People of the Book on qibla; following their desires after that command would place falsehood where truth belongs.
rows.anchor: فائدته ظاهرة، وهي بيان أول الوقت الذي وجب على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘you would then be among the wrongdoers,’ the clause answers the implied oath and indicates the omitted conditional answer; it cannot answer both oath and condition.
rows.anchor: قد ذكرنا أن هذه الجملة هي جواب القسم المحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It cannot answer both because an oath emphasizes without governing, whereas a condition governs and puts its clause in the jussive; the conditional answer would also require fa.
rows.anchor: فاقتضاء القسم على أنه لا عمل له فيه، لأن القسم إنما جيء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idhan sits between inna's subject and predicate to affirm their relation; placement first would suggest a link to the missing conditional result, while final placement would break the verse endings.
rows.anchor: فلو تقدمت، لتوهم أنها لتقرير النسبة التي بين الشرط والجواب المحذوف

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says idhan means answer and consequence, though grammarians differ over how to understand his statement.
rows.anchor: وقد نص سيبويه على أن معناها الجواب والجزاء. واختلف النحويون في فهم كلام سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes two uses of idhan: it may create a conditional causal link and govern a following future verb, or confirm a link already understood and therefore not govern.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن تدل على إنشاء الارتباط والشرط، بحيث لا يفهم الارتباط من غيرها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In its confirming use, idhan need not govern: removing it leaves the relation intelligible, and it can enter nominal clauses or move within the sentence.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثاني: أن تكون مؤكدة لجواب ارتبط بمتقدم، أو منبهة على مسبب شروط حصل في الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here idhan confirms an answer already linked with what precedes and does not govern; Abū Ḥayyān explains it because the particle occurs often in the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: فجاءت إذا في الآية مؤكدة للجواب المرتبط بما تقدم، وإنما قررت معناها هنا لأنها كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recipients of scripture may be Jewish and Christian scholars.
rows.anchor: هم علماء اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may instead be Jews who believed in the Messenger, such as Ibn Salām and others.
rows.anchor: أو من آمن برسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من اليهود، كابن سلام وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view takes them to be everyone who believed in the Messenger.
rows.anchor: أو من آمن به مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Depending on who is meant, ‘the Book’ may refer to the Torah, Gospel, both together, or the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: والكتاب: التوراة، أو الإنجيل، أو مجموعهما، أو القرآن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ātaynāhum is more eloquent than ūtū because it attributes the gift to God in the majestic first-person plural; related verbs of guidance and selection likewise express honor.
rows.anchor: ولفظ آتيناهم أبلغ من أوتوا، لإسناد الإيتاء إلى الله تعالى، معبرا عنه بنون العظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says ūtū can describe a gift without acceptance, while ātaynāhum is more often used where it is accepted, as in the verse listing Book, judgment, and prophethood.
rows.anchor: قيل: ولأن أوتوا قد يستعمل فيما لم يكن له قبول، وآتيناهم أكثر ما يستعمل فيما له قبول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When al-kitāb refers to more than one revealed book, it remains singular because it denotes the written object expressed by the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وإذ أريد بالكتاب أكثر من واحد، فوحد، لأنه صرف إلى المكتوب المعبر عنه بالمصدر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most apparent parsing makes ‘those We gave scripture’ the subject and ‘they recognize him’ its predicate; other parses make the clause an adjunct, apposition, or explicative parenthesis.
rows.anchor: والظاهر هو الإعراب الأول، لاستقلال الكلام جملة منعقدة من مبتدأ وخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternative parses make alladhīna genitive as an adjective or apposition, or nominative or accusative after an omitted introductory word; then yaʿrifūnahu is circumstantial with either object of ‘gave.’
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون الذين مجرورا على أنه صفة للظالمين، أو على أنه بدل من الظالمين

rows.speaker: مجاهِد وقتادة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Ibn ʿAbbās identify the object pronoun in ‘they recognize him’ as the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والضمير المنصوب في يعرفونه عائد على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، قاله مجاهد وقتادة وغيرهما.

rows.speaker: الزجاج والتبريزي والزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj chooses the Prophet as the pronoun's referent, al-Tabrīzī strengthens that choice, and al-Zamakhsharī leads with it.
rows.anchor: واختاره الزجاج، ورجحه التبريزي، وبدأ به الزمخشري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says they know the Prophet plainly, distinguishing him from others by his identifying description; the context supplies the unmentioned antecedent and conveys his fame.
rows.anchor: يعرفونه معرفة جلية، يميزون بينه وبين غيره بالوصف المعين المشخص.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the claim that the pronoun anticipates an unmentioned noun: the passage shifts from addressing the Prophet to speaking of the scripture recipients in the third person.
rows.anchor: فقد اتضح بما ذكرناه أنه ليس من باب الإضمار قبل الذكر، وأنه من باب الالتفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift addresses people after the Prophet: scripture bearers chosen to carry revelation know the Prophet, his truth, and the commanded qibla change because his description is written in Torah and Gospel.
rows.anchor: يعرفون هذا الذي خاطبناه في الآي السابقة وأمرناه ونهيناه، لا يشكون في معرفته، ولا في صدق أخباره

rows.speaker: عمر وعبد الله بن سلام
rows.claim: Umar asked Ibn Salām how this recognition worked; Ibn Salām said he recognized Muhammad on sight even more surely than his own son, testified that scripture described him as God's true Messenger, and Umar affirmed him; another version says Umar kissed his head.
rows.anchor: يا عمر، لقد عرفته حين رأيته، كما أعرف ابني، ومعرفتي بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم أشد من معرفتي بابني.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronoun refers to the Prophet, one interpretation is recognition of his face and distinguishing features, not his lineage.
rows.anchor: فقيل: المراد معرفة الوجه وتميزه، لا معرفة حقيقة النسب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation of recognizing the Prophet is knowing his truthfulness and prophethood.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى يعرفون صدقه ونبوته.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وابن جريج والربيع
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Rabīʿ take the pronoun as referring to the truth, namely the turn toward the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير عائد على الحق الذي هو التحول إلى الكعبة، قاله ابن عباس وقتادة أيضا، وابن جريج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations make the pronoun refer to the Qurʾān or to the knowledge itself.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عائد على القرآن. وقيل: على العلم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes it as the Kaaba's status as the qibla of Abraham and earlier prophets, a fact known only to scholars.
rows.anchor: وقيل: على كون البيت الحرام قبلة إبراهيم ومن قبله من الأنبياء، وهذه المعرفة مختصة بالعلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source of recognition depends on the referent: the Prophet is known by sight or description; the Qurʾān by scriptural confirmation; and the qibla or change through Qurʾān and the Messenger's miracle-supported report.
rows.anchor: فإن تعلقت المعرفة بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، فيكون حصولها بالرؤية والوصف، أو بالقرآن
